About the circle

Why this group exists

I'm a Palestinian-American living in the Boston area who picked up tatreez as a way of connecting with my Palestinian heritage and creating special projects to share with my loved ones. My mom's family are Nakba survivors from Safad, and my dad's family is from Jerusalem.

Tatreez was never meant to be a solitary craft. I wanted to build a beautiful community here in my hometown of Boston for people who love tatreez, and people who want to help keep the art alive.

Layan Ansari, Founder of Boston Tatreez Circle

What to expect

  • A warm, come-as-you-are stitching circle, no experience necessary.
  • Every other Saturday afternoon, all year long.
  • Background music and easy conversation while we stitch.
  • Sweets at every gathering, courtesy of Layan.
  • New to tatreez? This beginner's guide has everything you need to get started.

Where it comes from

A brief history of tatreez

Tatreez is "an artistic language that vocalizes indigenous stories," writes Jenna Abuelhaija, one that pushes back against narratives which deny Palestinians' cultural and geographic presence in their homeland.

Tatreez, the Arabic word for embroidery, refers to the cross-stitch work Palestinian women have practiced for centuries, traditionally passed from mother to daughter. Worked by hand onto the thobe, the traditional embroidered dress, tatreez uses geometric motifs drawn from daily life: cypress trees, orange blossoms, birds, and the shapes of the land itself. Historically, a woman's home village could often be read in the colors and patterns she stitched, since each region across Palestine developed its own distinct visual style.

After the Nakba of 1948 displaced hundreds of thousands of Palestinians from their homes, tatreez took on new meaning. Patterns once tied to a specific village became something diaspora families carried with them into exile, a way of holding onto memory and place when the land itself was out of reach. Today, tatreez is practiced across Palestine and its diaspora alike, as craft, as storytelling, and as an enduring act of cultural memory. In 2021, UNESCO recognized the art of embroidery in Palestine as part of humanity's Intangible Cultural Heritage.
